description:
Team of Undergraduate Students - sophomores.

We are working across aerospace engineering, physics and computer science, with a shared interest in astrophysics and infrared astronomy. We don’t build for the judges; we build for the person who’ll use our tool at 2 AM and spot something moving that no one’s seen. We seek members skilled in astrophysics, frontend (JavaScript/Aladin), Python/astropy and UI/UX design.

“You see, but you do not observe.”
Max Team Size - 4 to 5.
summary:
ORBITAL turns NASA’s newest all-sky survey into something anyone can watch. Type any sky position, or pick one of 19 ready targets, and ORBITAL plays every real SPHEREx near-infrared image of that spot as a short video, pulled live from NASA/IPAC IRSA. Moving stars, brown dwarfs, asteroids and pulsing stars jump out at a glance.

It meets the challenge: all five required targets play with real data, and a backup copy means the demo works even when the archive is down. Unlike a blink, ORBITAL guards against a SPHEREx trap: each image sees a slightly different colour, so a red star can seem to brighten when nothing changed. “Same colour only” compares like with like, and Gaia overlays show where each star should be.

Why it matters: SPHEREx’s archive is built for specialists. ORBITAL lets students, teachers and citizen scientists see the sky change for themselves, and check every frame at NASA.

WEBSITE LINK - https://planet-x-and-sphere-x-orbital.astrophysics.workers.dev

Previous Web - https://planet-x-and-sphere-x-orbital.4neesh-edu.workers.dev


GITHUB LINK - https://github.com/Ed-Aneesh/Planet-X-and-SPHEREx---ORBITAL

Summary:

ORBITAL is a free website that turns NASA's SPHEREx near-infrared sky images of any patch of sky and turns them into an interactive time-lapse. 

You type in a position, or pick one of our 19 famous targets. We find every SPHEREx exposure of that spot, clean them up, line them up, and play them like a flipbook. Around the player, we add older NASA images from 2MASS (about 1999) and AllWISE (2010), Gaia stars, and known asteroids. If a dot seems to be moving, you can check it in seconds instead of having to move between multiple different astronomy tools.

Our approach and why it is unique:

Most blink tools treat a sky time-lapse as pictures in date order. SPHEREx doesn’t work like that, and our whole design starts from that fact. Every pixel has a where, a when and a which colour, and we only trust a change on screen when we can show it isn’t an instrument effect.

  • Science first, then pictures. SPHEREx looks through linear variable filters, which are filters whose wavelength changes across the detector. The same star is therefore seen in a different colour in each exposure, and a plain flipbook can turn that colour change into fake brightening. We read each frame’s real wavelength from its own file and let you compare only like with like. We call this the same-colour rule.
  • Time, colour and history are separate dials. One patch can be viewed by date (Time), by wavelength (Colour), across 27 years of NASA missions (Mission), or two frames at a time (Compare). Each view answers one question, so they never get mixed up by accident.
  • The screen is honest. The “Can I trust a change here?” card tells you what’s behind what you’re looking at: the wavelength spread, the expected motion, flagged pixels, known asteroids and the data release. Damaged pixels are shown openly as masked holes rather than smoothed over.
  • Older surveys give us a long baseline. SPHEREx has only flown since 2025. By putting 2MASS and AllWISE images on the exact same pixel grid as SPHEREx, a star that moves less than a pixel a year becomes an obvious jump over the decades.
  • We checked our work against Gaia. We measured the motion of the fast-moving stars among our challenge targets from our own images and compared the results with Gaia and published values. They agree within 1.2σ on the 16-year baseline. Barnard’s Star, for example, comes out at 10.6 ± 0.25″/yr against 10.4 in the literature.
  • Real data, and it keeps working. Sky Probe always asks NASA/IPAC IRSA live. Star Vault plays a saved copy of the same IRSA files, so the demo still works if the archive is slow.
  • Built for the people who vet discoveries. Our design target is the citizen scientist, such as Backyard Worlds and NASA’s SPHEREx volunteer projects. That means shareable links, one screen instead of many tools, and every technical term explained in plain words.

The challenge and our targets

The challenge asks for a tool where you enter a position and see a time series of SPHEREx images played like a video. We went further, but the core is exactly that. All five required targets work on real data:

  • Barnard’s Star
  • Epsilon Indi B
  • WISE 0855−0714
  • RW Aurigae
  • R Draconis

Everything runs on real SPHEREx DR1 and Quick Release 3 images, pulled live from NASA/IPAC IRSA. There is no mock data anywhere.

The explorer

The explorer has three doors. The first two lead into the same player, and the third takes you from looking to measuring.

  • Star Vault is for instant, guided exploration. It holds 19 curated targets on a spinning ring: the five challenge targets plus 14 others that move, pulse, flare or exploded. It plays our saved copy of real IRSA files, so it works even when the archive is down.
  • Sky Probe is for the whole sky. Enter any RA/Dec (degrees or hh:mm:ss), a radius up to 0.25°, any band from D1 to D6, and any date range, for up to 400 exposures. It asks IRSA live, so new weekly SPHEREx data show up automatically.
  • Science Lab is for measuring. Once you’ve seen that something changes, the Lab tells you how much, with an error on every number: brightness in each exposure, a spectral energy distribution, and a variability analysis. It opens on the same target you picked on the home ring. The full details are in the Science Lab section below.

A few things make getting started easy:

  • Interactive sky map. Click anywhere on an all-sky map and the form fills itself in. Challenge targets, movers, variables, asteroids and deep fields appear as coloured dots.
  • Asteroid presets. 100 Hekate, 433 Eros, 10 Hygiea, 52 Europa and 24 Themis, each with the exact dates and band where SPHEREx caught them. We checked every one with IRSA’s Moving Object Search. It’s a way to see a real moving object in seconds.
  • Deep-field presets. The North and South Ecliptic Pole fields, where SPHEREx looks on every orbit, give you hundreds of visits to one patch. They’re ideal for stacking.
  • Moving-target support. For a typed position you can add proper motion (mas/yr) and an epoch. Named targets use catalogue motion. Either way, a fast star like Barnard’s Star stays centred on every date, because each frame is centred where the star was at that exposure’s time.
  • Home-page handoff. Every Vault, Probe and Lab link carries the target shown on the home ring, so nothing needs retyping.

Six ways to look at one patch

  • Time shows frames in date order, with an optional “Same colour only” switch that keeps frames within 1% in wavelength. It answers: did it move or change?
  • Colour shows one visit, with frames in wavelength order. It answers: what is it made of? This is not a variability view.
  • Mission shows 2MASS (about 1999), then AllWISE (2010), then SPHEREx, all on the same pixels. It answers: has it moved over 16 to 27 years?
  • Compare lets you blink or subtract any two frames. It blocks pairs more than 1% apart in wavelength and offers the closest match instead. It answers: what exactly changed between two dates?
  • Trail puts chosen images into one picture, coloured by date from blue (earliest) to red (latest). Still things look white. A mover leaves a rainbow trail.
  • Grid arranges every image by date (rows) and colour (columns). It answers: what has SPHEREx seen here, and what hasn’t it seen yet?

Checks and overlays on the player

  • Gaia stars. ESA Gaia DR3 stars, each moved to the exact date of every frame. A circle around a dot means it’s a known star. A dot without one deserves a look.
  • Predicted position. Where a moving star should be on each date, with its speed (for example 10.39″/yr) and a 10-year arrow.
  • Known asteroids. NASA/JPL’s Small-Body Identification service lists every catalogued asteroid and comet in the patch on each date, with names and error bars.
  • Missing data and flags. Pixels the SPHEREx pipeline distrusts (cosmic rays, saturation, ghosts, persistence) are shown honestly, alongside your own flags.
  • Frame labels. Band, wavelength, UTC date and data release are burned onto every frame.
  • “Can I trust a change here?” card. Live verdicts on colour spread, expected motion, flagged pixels, sampling and data release, plus a note on what the current view can’t tell you.
  • Check it at NASA/IRSA. One-click buttons open IRSA’s own SPHEREx Data Explorer, Moving Object Search and Spectrophotometry Tool for the same spot.
  • Where in the sky. A zoomable Aladin Lite atlas (2MASS, AllWISE and DSS backgrounds) shows the patch in context.
  • Measure the motion. Click the star in a 1999 or 2010 image and in SPHEREx, and ORBITAL gives you its proper motion in mas/yr with an uncertainty, compared against the catalogue.
  • Player controls. Auto-play at a speed you choose, frame buttons, a full-screen theatre view, swipe and pinch on phones, and keyboard shortcuts (press ? for the list).

The analysis toolbox, sharing and export

Sixteen tools work on the same loaded frames, grouped as View, Analyse, 3D and sky, and Save.

View

  • Gallery shows every frame side by side, so you can see the entire series at once.
  • Visit stacks add up the exposures of each survey pass to beat the noise, so faint objects appear.
  • Swipe lets you drag a line between two dates for an intuitive before-and-after.

Analyse

  • Difference shows later minus earlier, so only change survives. Movers leave a dark-and-bright pair, and variables leave a single spot.
  • Motion trail gives each visit its own colour, so a mover becomes a rainbow.
  • Measure motion lets you click an object and fit its speed and direction, with an uncertainty, checked against Gaia.
  • Signal-to-noise shows what stands above the noise, separating real sources from noise.
  • Wavelength window keeps one slice of wavelengths, which enforces the same-colour rule by hand.
  • Spectrum and light curve shows brightness by colour and by date.
  • Colour picture combines up to six detectors in one image, which makes cold brown dwarfs stand out by colour.
  • Flags shows your flags plus the pixels the pipeline distrusts, to help prevent false discoveries.

3D and sky

  • Spectral cube shows the data as x, y and wavelength, which makes SPHEREx’s three-dimensional nature visible.
  • Brightness landscape turns brightness into mountains you can spin.
  • Targets in 3D places all 19 targets around the Sun so distances become visible.
  • Planetarium shows the patch on a planetarium dome, so you see where it sits in the real sky.

Save

  • Report and export produces a GIF, video, CSV, FITS file and a report, so results can leave the website.

Sharing and guidance

  • Copy link. The URL holds the target, band, radius, view and overlays. Opening it reloads the same view, so a volunteer can paste it in a forum or a teacher can drop it in a slide.
  • Story mode. A five-step guided tour of the loaded target.
  • “Which band?” advisor. Recommends the detector (D1 to D6) for your target and explains why. For example, WISE 0855 only shines beyond about 3.9 µm, so it points you to D6.
  • FITS export. The aligned frames and visit stacks come out as a FITS file that astronomers can open in DS9 or astropy.

Science Lab in detail

The explorer shows that something changes; the Science Lab measures how much, with an error on every number. It is the third door beside Star Vault and Sky Probe, and it has its own page (lab.html) and back-end package (backend/lab/). Under the hood it is a self-contained module, so nothing in the explorer depends on it.

The Lab runs as nine independent stages: Gaia, retrieve, calibrate, measure, uncertainty, DR1 cube, SED, variability and report. A live stage tracker and log show progress. A failing stage never hides the others, and the source of every input is recorded.

  • Aperture and PSF photometry. Brightness in every exposure two ways: a circle of pixels minus a sky ring, and a fit of SPHEREx’s own measured point-spread function (ePSF). We tested it unbiased on fake stars and on 16 real Tabby’s Star exposures, where the two methods agree to 0.5%.
  • Error budgets. Every value lists its statistical, systematic and shared error terms and their share, which shows what limits the result. Shared calibration errors correctly cancel in light curves.
  • Spectral energy distribution. Blackbody, power-law and two-component fits with full error covariance, giving temperature, radius, luminosity and bolometric flux. It combines SPHEREx (0.75 to 5 µm) with Gaia XP optical spectra and warns when a model fits badly.
  • Variability. A per-band, colour-corrected light curve, a Lomb–Scargle periodogram, false-alarm probability, a sampling-window check and fractional variability. It removes SPHEREx’s colour effect before looking for change, and matches astropy to 10⁻¹⁴.
  • DR1 all-sky spectral cube. The spectrum at any position from IRSA’s 102-channel cube, reading only the bytes it needs. It works as an independent cross-check and warns when a neighbouring star contaminates the aperture.
  • Gaia DR3 integration. Parallax, distance, proper motion, radial velocity, 3-D space velocity, stellar parameters and the XP spectrum, with epoch propagation that matches astropy and ERFA to under 0.1 mas.
  • Downloads. The full result as JSON and the photometry table as CSV, so researchers can reuse it.

The Lab uses the same Python and NumPy back end and vanilla-JS front end, with its own self-test (python main.py --lab-selftest, 27 checks). Its data are SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 cutouts and ePSF tables, the DR1 spectral cube (doi:10.26131/IRSA679), Gaia DR3 (ESA archive and IRSA Gator), and Gaia XP spectra (GAVO Heidelberg).

How it works: the data pipeline

Every request runs the same nine-step chain on the server, from a position to a cleaned, aligned set of frames. 

  • Find every SPHEREx exposure covering the position. We ask two IRSA services at the same time, TAP (an SQL-like catalogue query) and SIA (Simple Image Access), and the first useful answer wins. One slow service never blocks the user.
  • Pick one calibration. DR1 and Quick Release 3 are used together because IRSA processes them uniformly. Older QR2 and QR1 data are only a fallback and are never mixed in. When there are duplicates, we keep the newest copy.
  • Choose frames evenly spread in time and group them into survey visits. A visit is a pass about six months apart, never longer than 14 days, so the ecliptic-pole deep fields still split into visits.
  • Download cutouts. We take only the small square around the target from each 2040×2040 image. The download stops after the layers we need and skips the roughly 4.9 MB PSF layer. The wavelength table is fetched once per detector and reused. That’s about 0.1 MB per frame instead of about 5 MB.
  • Clean. We subtract the zodiacal-light model (sunlight scattered by Solar System dust, supplied in each file) and mask bad pixels using the flag names in each file’s own header: cosmic rays, saturation, hot and cold pixels, persistence, ghosts and streaks.
  • Align. Every frame is reprojected onto one north-up grid using the file’s own sky coordinates and optical-distortion terms. Moving stars are centred on their position at that exposure’s date.
  • Measure the colour. We read the exact wavelength at the target in every frame from the file’s wavelength table.
  • Display. All frames share one brightness stretch (ZScale plus asinh), so a brightness change on screen is real and not a per-frame contrast trick.
  • Add context. Gaia DR3 stars, 2MASS and AllWISE images on the same grid, and known asteroids from NASA/JPL.

Behind the scenes: what keeps it reliable

  • Search and result caches. Archive searches are remembered for hours and finished results are kept on disk, so a second view of a target is instant.
  • Star Vault saved copy. IRSA files are stored on Google Drive and read through a service account, so the demo works with IRSA down.
  • Honest failure messages. “No coverage yet”, “nothing in that date range (available: …)”, and clear explanations of archive timeouts, so the user always knows why.
  • Polite to IRSA. Parallel downloads are limited, failed requests retry with back-off, and downloads cancel when the page closes.
  • Self-test. “python main.py --selftest” runs 49 offline checks with fake cutouts in the real file layout, covering alignment, motion, flags and the API.
  • Independent validation. “python main.py --validate” uses raw FITS, astropy WCS and a 2-D Gaussian fit, a separate chain, so our motion numbers are checked twice.
  • No-install backend. A Python standard-library web server, with astropy optional and a built-in NumPy fallback, so it runs even on locked-down Windows PCs.

Built-In Learning and Storytelling

ORBITAL is designed so a newcomer can understand what they are looking at within a minute:

  • Clear home page: Opens with a simple promise ("Watch the infrared sky and spot what moves"), an animated blink preview, and key mission stats (102 channels, 6 detectors, 19 targets, all-sky).
  • Pipeline explainer: Walks judges and students through how raw archive data becomes a calibrated video.
  • Target ring and fact cards: Displays RA/Dec, distance, proper motion, and verified fun facts for all 19 targets, with an "Open in explorer" button that sends you to Vault, Probe, or Lab.
  • Interactive spectrum bar: Maps SPHEREx's 0.75–5.0 µm coverage across all 6 detectors and 102 channels, highlighting water, CO₂, and CO ice absorption bands alongside hydrogen lines.
  • Mission comparison table: Contrasts SPHEREx, WISE/NEOWISE, and 2MASS across wavelength, cadence, pixel scale, and best scientific use.
  • Searchable A–Z glossary: Defines every astronomical and archive acronym in one or two sentences for non-astronomers.
  • Science and credits documentation: Explains the same-colour rule, sub-pixel astrometry, epoch propagation, validation results for all 19 targets, known limitations, 6 required agency acknowledgements, and 66 cited sources.
  • Accessible design: Supports dark/light themes and mobile touch gestures (swipe and pinch-to-zoom).

Tech stack

We kept the stack deliberately light: a plain web front end and a Python back end, with no framework to install, so it runs on any laptop and can be hosted for free.

  • Front end: HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript, with no framework and no build step. It covers the home page, Star Vault, Sky Probe, Science, Credits and Lab.
  • Graphics: HTML Canvas 2D and SVG for the player, overlays, difference images, trails, 3-D views and charts.
  • Sky atlas: Aladin Lite 3.8.2 (CDS Strasbourg, shipped with the site) plus HiPS mirrors from CDS, ESA ESASky, CSIRO CASDA and China-VO.
  • Back end: Python 3 with a threaded standard-library HTTP server, serving both the website and the JSON API.
  • Science: NumPy and Astropy (FITS, WCS, ZScale, times), with our own NumPy fallback for WCS and FITS.
  • Archive access: requests, with IVOA TAP, SIA v2, VOTable and the IRSA cutout service.
  • Catalogues: the ESA Gaia archive (TAP), IRSA Gator, NASA/JPL Small-Body Identification API, and SIMBAD.
  • Saved data: Google Drive API v3 with a google-auth service account.
  • Export: our own FITS writer, GIF encoder and CSV.
  • Testing: the offline self-test (49 checks), an astropy-based validation script, and headless-browser checks.
  • Hosting: Render (render.yaml), and it runs equally well on a local PC.
  • Fonts: Archivo, Instrument Serif, Manrope and Space Mono (Google Fonts, OFL).

Data

Every image and catalogue in ORBITAL is open data from NASA or a partner agency. The full list with citations is on the site’s Credits page.

  • SPHEREx DR1 and Quick Release 3 spectral images (doi:10.26131/IRSA678, doi:10.26131/IRSA662), from NASA/JPL-Caltech and served by NASA/IPAC IRSA. Every frame in the player comes from here.
  • IRSA services (TAP, SIA, cutout service, Gator, Moving Object Search, SPHEREx Data Explorer) from NASA/IPAC, used for finding, cutting and checking data.
  • 2MASS All-Sky Atlas (about 1999), from NASA and NSF, UMass and IPAC, for the 27-year motion baseline.
  • WISE / AllWISE Atlas (2010 to 2011), from NASA, JPL and UCLA, for the 16-year baseline.
  • Gaia DR3, from ESA, for the known-star overlay and for validating our measured motions.
  • Small-Body Identification API, from NASA/JPL Solar System Dynamics, for known asteroids and comets in each frame.
  • Aladin Lite, SIMBAD and HiPS sky surveys, from CDS Strasbourg, for the sky atlas and object names.

Limitations

We say this on the site too, because a tool for spotting discoveries has to be clear about what it cannot prove.

  • A candidate is not a discovery. ORBITAL flags things worth a closer look. Confirming them needs professional follow-up.
  • Our proper motions are a check, not new science. Gaia measures them about 100 times better. Our point is that SPHEREx plus older NASA surveys can reproduce them, in a browser, for anyone.
  • Saturated stars bias position measurements. Mira, Betelgeuse and R Draconis are shown as masked holes rather than hidden.
  • Brightness isn’t compared across missions. 2MASS, WISE and SPHEREx use different filters, so only positions are compared.
  • Coverage grows weekly. SPHEREx sees each spot a few times per detector every six months, so a short date window (an asteroid over two or three days) holds about 10 to 20 images per band. We show all of them.
  • Star Vault is a frozen copy, about 3′ around each target. The newest weekly data and wide fields need Sky Probe.
  • Known-asteroid positions come from JPL’s fast predictions. We draw error bars when they exceed one pixel.
